newsitem.title: USA: US campaign fund hearings focus on foreign angle.
newsitem.headline: US campaign fund hearings focus on foreign angle.

text.p: A Democratic Party donor with links to India and a Japanese bank became the latest Asian players in the U.S. election fund-raising probe on Thursday as hearings focused on possible foreign efforts to sway the U.S. political process.

Sen. Susan Collins of Maine told the Senate campaign finance hearings that Democratic Party donor Yogesh Gandhi last year received cash transfers from a Japanese bank and suggested these may have covered his donations.
She spoke on the third day of hearings by the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, which is probing alleged campaign finance abuses during the 1996 presidential election.

Collins, a Republican committee member, said Gandhi gave the Democratic National Committee (DNC) $325,000 at a dinner in May 1996. The money was later returned by the DNC, which said it could not verify its source.

During the questioning of former DNC Finance Director Richard Sullivan, she said that in August 1996 Gandhi had testified in court that he had no funds in the United States and insufficent income to file U.S. income taxes.

"Would it surprise you to know ... committee investigators have uncovered a wire transfer from a Japanese bank for this amount into Mr. Gandhi's personal account?" Collins asked. "Is this yet another example of the DNC failing to do a sufficient job to screen a very large contribution that's coming in from a source that's never contributed before?"

The committee distributed copies of bank transfers to Gandhi worth $250,000 each on May 20 and May 23, 1996, originating from a person or entity identified only as "Yoshio Tanaka." Under U.S. law, foreigners and foreign companies are generally barred from making political contributions.

There are exceptions for foreigners who are legal U.S. residents, like Gandhi, or for subsidiaries of foreign companies that have substantial U.S. operations and could have covered their donations from the subsidiaries' U.S. income.

Collins also said Gandhi had been rebuffed by the White House when he sought a meeting with President Bill Clinton but that after he made the $325,000 donation the DNC arranged for him to meet Clinton at the May 1996 dinner.

Announcing that it had returned the donation last year, the DNC said Gandhi, a distant relative of Mahatma Gandhi, had presented Clinton with a life-sized bust of the Indian spiritual leader at the dinner.
The Senate hearings, which began on Tuesday, have focused on the possibility that foreign countries sought to influence the U.S. political process by targeted donations during the 1996 campaign.
Sen. Fred Thompson, the Tennessee Republican who chairs the panel, opened the hearings by saying he believed China plotted to influence U.S. politics and foreign policy.

Thursday's sessions focused on the role of John Huang, the Democratic fund-raiser who arranged the May 1996 dinner that Gandhi attended. Huang, a former Commerce Department official, arranged some of the DNC's most controversial fund-raising events during the 1996 campaign, including a dinner and a coffee that brought Clinton into contact with foreign citizens.
A U.S. citizen of Taiwanese descent, Huang raised $3.4 million during his nine months with the DNC, which has returned $1.6 million that it deemed questionable.

He has so far refused to testify but has said he might do so if the committee were to to give him "limited immunity" that would essentially protect him from any criminal charges except those concerning espionage or the passing of secrets.
